text: Shot count is the one knob in a hybrid workflow that directly trades real money for statistical precision, on a well-defined mathematical curve. This lesson works that curve out in actual numbers, so how many shots should I use stops being a guess.

A measured expectation value's standard error scales as one over the square root of shots — precision improves with the square root of shot count, not linearly. We'll price out a real precision target, and see why running more shots than your use case needs is pure wasted spend, not extra safety.

Here's the relationship in real numbers. Five hundred shots: a standard error around four and a half percent. A thousand shots: about three percent. Four thousand shots — four times as many — cuts that error to one point five eight percent: exactly half. To halve your error, you need four times the shots. For a ten-times improvement in precision, you need a hundred times the shots.

Here's a real measured value from IBM Quantum's documentation — exactly the kind of number this standard-error arithmetic exists to qualify. Reporting a number like this with no uncertainty attached is the Chapter 1 mistake all over again.

And here's what happens when a shot budget is genuinely too thin for what you're trying to see — real measured noise from IBM's own hardware. A shot-budget decision should start from what precision your actual use case needs, not from a round number that sounds thorough. Padding from twenty-five hundred to ten thousand shots across a two-hundred-task job can cost an extra thirteen hundred fifty dollars for precision your application's own decision threshold doesn't require.
